title: Dispatcher occupancy & latchbench: multi-tenant kernel handoff notes
content:
Context:
These are notes from an exploratory bench we ran to diagnose high p99 spikes that correlate with kernel handoffs under mixed-precision workloads. Instead of the usual throughput/latency tables I focused on GPU lane occupancy, the dispatcher latch wait time (internal name: latch_wait_ns), and kernel-switch frequency per request. This is messy, lots of raw logs and heuristics — notes to self and the SREs.

Goal / hypothesis:
- Hypothesis: when the dispatcher switches kernels (AWQ <-> GPTQ <-> INT8 runtime paths) on a per-request basis, we see transient occupancy imbalance on the SM lanes that causes short (<5ms) but high-amplitude p99 latency spikes.
- Secondary: multi-tenant blends with many small requests increase kernel-switch churn making the dispatcher latch contended.

Test harness and config:
- Branch: local/dispatcher-occupancy-probe (see PR above).
- Models: llama-13b (GPTQ), fed through two quant variants: awq-v1 and gptq-fast. Also tested int8-packed path and fp8-staging.
- Hardware: 8xA100-40GB, single GPU tests pinned to GPU0 to remove cross-GPU variance.
- Runtime kernels: kernel-amp-v3 (default), kernel-packed-int8-v1, awq-opt-kernel-2.
- Traffic shapes:
  - shape-A: 60% small-chat (avg tokens 18), 40% long-context (avg tokens 1024) — bursty Poisson arrivals (lambda=40 reqs/s).
  - shape-B: many micro-requests — 200 reqs/s of avg 8 tokens (simulates PLG client).
- Multi-tenant mix: two logical tenants on same GPU; weight ratio 70/30.
- Instrumentation added:
  - latch_wait_ns: time dispatcher mutex/latch spends waiting before kernel handoff
  - kernel_switches_per_req: integer count
  - occupancy_skew_pct: computed from per-lane occupancy sample (max-min)/mean over a 10ms sliding window, expressed as percent
  - kv-cache-prefetch-wait: boolean flag when prefetch blocks kernel entry

Measurements collected:
- Standard: p50/p90/p99 generation latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU util.
- New metrics (sampled at 1ms): latch_wait_ns, occupancy_skew_pct, kernel_switches_per_req, active_kernels_set per epoch.
- Also collected microtraces from CUDA events for a subset of requests (10k).

Key observations (raw):
- Under shape-A (mixed short+long), p99 spikes correlate tightly with occupancy_skew_pct bursts. Typical pattern: occupancy_skew_pct jumps from ~8% baseline to 35-60% for 6–12 ms windows.
- Those windows nearly always coincide with latch_wait_ns > 2000us.
- kernel_switches_per_req distribution: median 0 (same kernel), 75th percentile 1, 99th percentile 3 under shape-A. The 99th percentile requests almost always show both high latch_wait_ns and occupancy skew.
- Shape-B (micro-requests) increases kernel_switch churn: 99th percentile kernel_switches_per_req = 6. p99 latency worsened by ~18% relative to single-tenant baseline.
- KV prefetch waits were present in ~12% of high-latch cases; prefetch can extend latch_wait_ns by 800–1200us in the worst cases.

Interpretation / why this matters:
- The dispatcher latch is currently a coarse-grained synchronization point used to serialize kernel swaps and protect the KV cache state. With frequent kernel swaps (due to per-request model variant routing or quant fallback), contention causes short windows where lane occupancy becomes imbalanced — some vector lanes run different kernel code paths or wait idle while others execute resulting in effective under-utilization and tail latency spikes.
- Even if overall GPU utilization stays high, occupancy skew kills tail latency because a small set of warps stall waiting for synchronized resources.

Triaged root causes (candidates):
1) Dispatcher lock granularity: we serialize too much; per-request kernel metadata and KV cache check are on the same critical section.
2) Kernel binary switching path is expensive: codegen or memory remap touching page tables or kernel-launch parameters that cause SM scheduling jitter.
3) KV-prefetch and cache-miss paths hold dispatcher latch while issuing async prefetches — blocking short-running requests.
4) Poor mapping of short requests to persistent kernel processes (no kernel pinning), leading to repeated kernel reinitialization.

Quick experiments run and outcomes:
- Removed KV-prefetch from latch path (offloaded to async thread): p99 decreased by ~9% and latch_wait_ns 99th dropped ~40% for shape-A. Suggests prefetch holding latch is real.
- Introduced kernel pinning (sticky kernels per tenant) for short requests: kernel_switches_per_req 99th reduced from 3->1 in shape-A, p99 improved ~12%.
- Rewrote dispatcher latch to a split-lock (metadata lock + cache lock) in branch: results looked promising in microbench but caused subtle cache-race in rare long-context flows — need more safety guards.

Unresolved weirdness / anomalies:
- Some p99 spikes still show occupancy_skew_pct high without high latch_wait_ns. In those cases, microtraces show long kernels executing (attention-heavy) concurrently with many small kernels; suggests scheduling interference at SM warp scheduler level that isn't mediated by our latch. Could be driver-level or kernel resource fragmentation (shared memory/register pressure).
- In one run kernel-packed-int8-v1 showed lower p99 but higher P50 than awq-opt-kernel-2; suggests packing reduces variance but increases per-token overhead for short requests. Tradeoff depends on request size distribution.

Actionable next steps (prioritized):
1) Short term (1–2 sprints):
   - Keep KV-prefetch off latch by default; release as opt-in removal. (Owner: Marco)
   - Rollout kernel pinning heuristics for tenants with >60% short requests. (Owner: Aisha)
   - Add extra metrics: per-SM warp-stall-counter snapshot (if driver exposes) and per-kernel shared-memory usage sample at launch. (Owner: Riley)
2) Medium term (2–3 sprints):
   - Implement safe split-lock + validation harness in CI: fuzz long-context flows to catch race conditions.
   - Evaluate lightweight kernel warm-pool so short requests reuse warmed kernels without full switch cost.
3) Long term:
   - Investigate kernel co-scheduling policies with Nvidia driver team (SM scheduler interference). Open ticket with HW vendor. (JIRA INF-3214)
   - Consider routing policy changes: collapse per-request quant-path variation by grouping short requests into a fast-path quant variant.

Notes to maintainers / ops:
- If you see sudden p99 regressions after deploy of kernel-packed-int8-v1, check latch_wait_ns and occupancy_skew_pct first.
- Use the replay harness present in /bench/replay/occupancy to replicate shape-A; add --trace-latches to collect latch traces.

Appendix: quick commands used
- run-replay: ./bench/replay --config configs/shape-A.yaml --duration 15m --trace-latches
- extract-latches: python tools/extract_latches.py --input traces/2027-07-12 --out summary.csv

Questions I still have (for the group):
- Is there a lightweight way to detect SM-level scheduling interference from userspace without full driver cooperation? (Riley: any kernels/tricks?)
- Should we prefer increasing batch sizes to reduce kernel switches, or is kernel pinning safer for latency-critical clients?
- Can we add a per-tenant sticky-kernel TTL that decays to avoid long-lived fragmentation?

Raw attachments / artifacts (where to find raw logs):
- traces: gs://redwood-internal/bench/occupancy/2027-07-12/ (10GB)
- kernel samples: s3://bench-samples/dispatcher-occupancy/kernel-samples-07-12.tar.gz

Summary (one-liner):
Short requests + per-request quant switching -> dispatcher latch contention + occupancy skew -> p99 tail. Early wins: remove prefetch from latch and apply kernel pinning heuristics.

-- Aisha
